questions.topicName: Cardiac - Compliance, Contractility, Preload, and Afterload
questions.stem: This curve plots developed tension/stroke volume against preload (end-diastolic volume or pressure). What physiologic principle does it depict?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The exponential rise of diastolic pressure with filling volume

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pressure-volume loop area representing stroke work

choices.label: D
choices.text: Afterload mismatch causing progressive fall in stroke volume

choices.label: E
choices.text: Autoregulation of coronary blood flow with perfusion pressure

explanation.summary: The rising, then plateauing, curve of force versus preload is the Frank-Starling mechanism: greater end-diastolic stretch increases actin-myosin overlap and contractile force until overstretch limits further gain.
explanation.whyCorrect: The rising, then plateauing, curve of force versus preload is the Frank-Starling mechanism: greater end-diastolic stretch increases actin-myosin overlap and contractile force until overstretch limits further gain.

questions.stem: These left ventricular pressure-volume loops show three beats with equal preload but progressively higher afterload (1 < 2 < 3). What happens to stroke volume as afterload rises?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Stroke volume decreases because the ventricle ejects against greater resistance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stroke volume increases as the aortic valve opens at a higher pressure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stroke volume is unchanged because preload is held constant

choices.label: D
choices.text: Contractility increases to fully compensate, keeping ejection fraction constant

choices.label: E
choices.text: End-diastolic volume falls with each successive beat

explanation.summary: With preload fixed, raising afterload forces the ventricle to reach a higher pressure before the aortic valve opens, so it ejects a smaller volume; end-systolic volume rises and stroke volume falls.
explanation.whyCorrect: With preload fixed, raising afterload forces the ventricle to reach a higher pressure before the aortic valve opens, so it ejects a smaller volume; end-systolic volume rises and stroke volume falls.

questions.stem: On these LV diastolic pressure-volume curves, the rightward-shifted red curve reaches a given end-diastolic volume at a lower pressure. What does this curve represent?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased compliance from a stiff, hypertrophied ventricle

explanation.summary: Compliance is the change in volume per change in pressure; a curve shifted right/down accommodates more volume at lower filling pressure, indicating increased compliance, whereas a steep left-shifted curve (higher EDP for the same EDV) indicates a stiff, less compliant ventricle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Compliance is the change in volume per change in pressure; a curve shifted right/down accommodates more volume at lower filling pressure, indicating increased compliance, whereas a steep left-shifted curve (higher EDP for the same EDV) indicates a stiff, less compliant ventricle.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Total tension equals passive tension minus active tension

choices.label: B
choices.text: Active tension arises only after passive tension plateaus

choices.label: C

questions.stem: This diagram shows oxygen consumption measured at the mouth, pulmonary artery saturation of 75%, and arterial saturation of 95%. Which method of determining cardiac output does it illustrate?

explanation.summary: The Fick principle calculates cardiac output by dividing whole-body oxygen consumption (VO2) by the arteriovenous oxygen content difference, here estimated from the mixed venous (PA, 75%) versus arterial (95%) saturations.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Fick principle calculates cardiac output by dividing whole-body oxygen consumption (VO2) by the arteriovenous oxygen content difference, here estimated from the mixed venous (PA, 75%) versus arterial (95%) saturations.

questions.topicName: Cardiac and Vascular Function Curves
questions.stem: On this venous return curve, the dashed lines show the effect of changing blood volume and venous tone. Increasing blood volume/venous tone shifts the x-axis intercept (mean circulatory filling pressure) in which direction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To the left, to a lower mean circulatory filling pressure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Downward with no change in intercept

choices.label: D
choices.text: The curve rotates without moving the intercept

choices.label: E
choices.text: To the right, to a higher mean circulatory filling pressure

explanation.summary: Adding volume or increasing venous tone raises the mean circulatory filling pressure (the x-intercept where venous return is zero), shifting the entire venous return curve rightward and upward and increasing venous return at any given right atrial pressure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adding volume or increasing venous tone raises the mean circulatory filling pressure (the x-intercept where venous return is zero), shifting the entire venous return curve rightward and upward and increasing venous return at any given right atrial pressure.

questions.topicName: Cardiac and Vascular Function Curves
questions.stem: These venous return curves illustrate the effect of changing afterload (arteriolar resistance). How does a decrease in afterload affect venous return at a given right atrial pressure?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Venous return increases (the curve shifts upward)

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mean circulatory filling pressure rises sharply

choices.label: E
choices.text: The mean circulatory filling pressure falls sharply

explanation.summary: Lowering arteriolar resistance (afterload) allows blood to flow more readily from arteries into veins and back to the heart, raising the venous return curve. Note that the x-intercept (MCFP) is relatively unchanged because total blood volume and venous tone are constant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lowering arteriolar resistance (afterload) allows blood to flow more readily from arteries into veins and back to the heart, raising the venous return curve. Note that the x-intercept (MCFP) is relatively unchanged because total blood volume and venous tone are constant.

questions.topicName: Cardiac and Vascular Function Curves
questions.stem: This plot superimposes the cardiac function curve and the vascular (venous return) function curve. Which relationship is true at their point of intersection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Venous return is at its theoretical maximum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mean circulatory filling pressure has been reached

explanation.summary: The system settles where the heart pumps out exactly what returns to it. At this intersection cardiac output equals venous return, defining the steady-state right atrial pressure and cardiac output for the given conditions.
explanation.whyCorrect: The system settles where the heart pumps out exactly what returns to it. At this intersection cardiac output equals venous return, defining the steady-state right atrial pressure and cardiac output for the given conditions.

questions.topicName: Cardiac and Vascular Function Curves
questions.stem: Starting from the central steady-state point, an increase in cardiac contractility moves the operating point toward which labeled point, and with what effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Point 2 - decreased cardiac output with increased right atrial pressure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Point 2 - increased cardiac output with increased right atrial pressure

choices.label: C
choices.text: The operating point does not move

choices.label: D
choices.text: Point 1 - decreased cardiac output with increased right atrial pressure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Point 1 - increased cardiac output with decreased right atrial pressure

explanation.summary: Increased contractility raises and steepens the cardiac function curve, so the intersection with the unchanged venous return curve moves up and to the left (point 1): cardiac output rises while right atrial pressure falls because the heart empties more effectively.

questions.topicName: Cardiac and Vascular Function Curves
questions.stem: From the central steady-state point, a decrease in afterload moves the operating point toward point 2. What happens to cardiac output and right atrial pressure?

choices.label: A

choices.label: C

questions.topicName: Cardiac and Vascular Function Curves
questions.stem: In this overlay of cardiac and vascular function curves, the red curve is markedly flattened and depressed compared with a normal individual (point A). What physiological state does this red 'cardiac function' curve represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A failing heart with reduced contractility

choices.label: E
choices.text: A normal heart with increased contractility

explanation.summary: A downward, flattened cardiac function curve indicates depressed contractility (heart failure): at any given filling pressure the heart generates less output, so the operating point shifts to a higher right atrial pressure with a lower cardiac output.
explanation.whyCorrect: A downward, flattened cardiac function curve indicates depressed contractility (heart failure): at any given filling pressure the heart generates less output, so the operating point shifts to a higher right atrial pressure with a lower cardiac output.

questions.topicName: Cardiac and Vascular Function Curves
questions.stem: This schematic depicts blood moving from the veins (venous return) through the heart into the arteries (cardiac output) as a closed loop. If venous tone increases in this system, what happens to venous return and cardiac output at steady state?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both venous return and cardiac output increase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cardiac output increases but venous return is unchanged

choices.label: C
choices.text: Venous return increases but cardiac output falls

explanation.summary: Because the circulation is a closed loop, cardiac output must equal venous return over time. Increased venous tone raises the mean circulatory filling pressure and augments venous return; the heart then pumps this extra volume forward, so cardiac output rises to match.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the circulation is a closed loop, cardiac output must equal venous return over time. Increased venous tone raises the mean circulatory filling pressure and augments venous return; the heart then pumps this extra volume forward, so cardiac output rises to match.

questions.topicName: Cardiac and Vascular Function Curves
questions.stem: This curve plots cardiac output against left ventricular end-diastolic volume, rising steeply and then plateauing. Which physiological principle does it illustrate?

explanation.summary: The Frank-Starling relationship states that increased ventricular filling (preload/EDV) stretches the myocardium and increases stroke volume and cardiac output, until the curve plateaus. This intrinsic mechanism matches output to venous return on a beat-to-beat basis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Frank-Starling relationship states that increased ventricular filling (preload/EDV) stretches the myocardium and increases stroke volume and cardiac output, until the curve plateaus. This intrinsic mechanism matches output to venous return on a beat-to-beat basis.

questions.imageRef: repic-685_Brick Exchange - Cardiac and Vascular Function Curves_p3_1.png

questions.topicName: Cardiac and Vascular Function Curves
questions.stem: On this cardiac (Frank-Starling) function curve, the upper dashed line represents an upward, leftward shift. Which intervention would produce this change?

explanation.summary: An upward shift reflects increased contractility (positive inotropy). Sympathetic beta-1 stimulation, catecholamines, and digoxin raise contractility, so the heart generates more output at any given end-diastolic volume. Ischemia and beta-blockade depress the curve.
explanation.whyCorrect: An upward shift reflects increased contractility (positive inotropy). Sympathetic beta-1 stimulation, catecholamines, and digoxin raise contractility, so the heart generates more output at any given end-diastolic volume. Ischemia and beta-blockade depress the curve.

questions.imageRef: repic-686_Brick Exchange - Cardiac and Vascular Function Curves_p5_1.png

questions.topicName: Cardiac and Vascular Function Curves
questions.stem: On this cardiac function curve, the lower dashed line represents increased afterload. Which condition would shift the curve downward in this manner?

explanation.summary: Increased afterload (higher aortic/arterial pressure the ventricle must eject against) lowers stroke volume for any given end-diastolic volume, depressing the cardiac function curve. Aortic stenosis and systemic hypertension raise afterload; vasodilators and low-resistance states lower it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Increased afterload (higher aortic/arterial pressure the ventricle must eject against) lowers stroke volume for any given end-diastolic volume, depressing the cardiac function curve. Aortic stenosis and systemic hypertension raise afterload; vasodilators and low-resistance states lower it.

questions.topicName: Cardiac and Vascular Function Curves
questions.stem: On this venous return curve, the x-axis intercept (arrow, where venous return falls to zero) marks a specific pressure. Under what condition is this pressure measured?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When right atrial pressure becomes negative

choices.label: B
choices.text: At the moment of maximal cardiac output

choices.label: E
choices.text: At the point of maximal venous return

explanation.summary: The x-intercept is the mean circulatory filling pressure: the pressure everywhere in the vasculature when the heart stops and flow ceases (normally ~7 mmHg). It reflects blood volume and venous compliance/tone, and it is the driving pressure for venous return.
explanation.whyCorrect: The x-intercept is the mean circulatory filling pressure: the pressure everywhere in the vasculature when the heart stops and flow ceases (normally ~7 mmHg). It reflects blood volume and venous compliance/tone, and it is the driving pressure for venous return.

questions.topicName: Pressure Volume (PV) Loops
questions.stem: In this left ventricular pressure-volume loop, the green loop represents increased preload. How does raising preload change the loop (contractility and afterload held constant)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Stroke volume falls as end-systolic volume rises

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peak systolic pressure needed to eject falls markedly

choices.text: End-diastolic volume and stroke volume both increase

choices.text: End-diastolic volume falls and the loop narrows
